paraphrase: When little of the Kṛta age remained, the great asura Maya, wishing to know the supreme, holy and secret knowledge — the foremost Vedāṅga, the whole cause of the courses of the lights — propitiated the Sun with severe austerity. Pleased, the Sun himself gave Maya the account of the planets: 'I have no time to tell it and none can bear my brilliance; this person, my portion, will tell you all.' Having appointed that portion he vanished, and the man spoke to the bowing Maya: 'Hear the highest knowledge told by Vivasvant himself to the great seers in age after age. This is that same original śāstra which the Sun spoke of old; only the difference of time arises through the turning of the ages.'

paraphrase: Time is of two kinds: the time that makes an end of the worlds, and another time whose nature is reckoning. paraphrase: Twelve thousand divine years make a caturyuga, that is 4,320,000 solar years, including its dawn and twilight portions. The arrangement of Kṛta and the rest follows the feet of dharma: a tenth of the yuga multiplied by four, three, two and one gives Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, each with a sixth as its twilights. Seventy-one yugas make a manvantara, with a twilight of a Kṛta's length at its end, a flood; fourteen Manus with their junctions, and a junction at the start, make a kalpa of a thousand yugas — a day of Brahmā, destroying beings, with a night of equal length. His life is a hundred such years; half of it has passed, and this is the first kalpa of the remainder.

paraphrase: Vāsudeva is the supreme Brahman; his embodiment is the supreme Person, unmanifest, without qualities, peaceful, beyond the twenty-five principles, imperishable. Entering nature, as Saṅkarṣaṇa he first created the waters and cast his seed into them; it became a golden egg wrapped in darkness, in which Aniruddha first became manifest — the Hiraṇyagarbha of the Veda, called Āditya as the first and Sūrya as the begetter. He is the highest light beyond darkness, the self of time and maker of time, the all-pervading self in whom all rests; the Ṛk verses are his disc, the Sāmans his rays, the Yajus his form. Mounting a chariot whose wheel is the year, yoked with the seven metres as horses, he circles the worlds. Of his threefold immortal hidden being one quarter became manifest; he created Brahmā as the ego-principle for the creation, gave him the Vedas, set him in the egg and himself circles, sustaining.

paraphrase: Brahmā, bearing the form of the ego-principle, set his mind on creation: from his mind the moon was born, from his eyes the sun, treasury of light; from mind came ether, then air, fire, water and earth, each with one more quality. Fire-and-Soma are the sun and moon; then Mars and the rest were born in order from fire, earth, ether, water and air. The Lord again divided himself twelvefold as the signs and twenty-sevenfold as the asterisms; then he made the moving and unmoving world, beginning with the gods, and assigned to planets, stars, earth, gods, demons, men and siddhas their places according to quality and action, as seen in the Veda.

paraphrase: The egg of Brahmā is hollow, and within it the worlds bhūr, bhuvaḥ and the rest are like two joined bowls forming a sphere. Within it the orbits lie one below another — Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, the Moon — and below them siddhas, vidyādharas and clouds. In the middle of the egg the earth-globe stands in space, bearing the supreme supporting power of Brahman. Within it are the seven netherworlds of nāgas and asuras; Meru, a golden mountain, passes through the middle of the globe and projects on both sides; above it dwell the gods with Indra and the great seers, below it the asuras, hostile to one another; the ocean surrounds the earth like a girdle dividing gods from asuras.
